gaps.text: Immunity of UNO and its agencies
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibition of Discrimination on Certain Grounds – Article 15
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Word ‘discrimination’ means to make adverse distinction
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Word ‘only’ means discrimination on other grounds not prohibited
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Second provision of Article 15: no citizen subjected to disability on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth regarding access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment; use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, places of public resort
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibition under second provision applies to both State and private individuals (first provision only against State)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Four exceptions to non-discrimination under Article 15
children: Exception (a): State can make special provision for women and children (e.g., reservation in local bodies, free education for children)
Exception (b): State can make special provision for socially and educationally backward classes or SCs and STs (e.g., reservation in public educational institutions)

Exception (c): State can make special provision for advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes or SCs/STs regarding admission to educational institutions including private (aided or unaided) except minority institutions – added by 93rd Amendment Act, 2005

Exception (d): State can make special provision for economically weaker sections (EWS) including reservation of up to 10% seats in educational institutions (including private aided/unaided except minority institutions) – added by 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: EWS reservation is in addition to existing reservations
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: EWS to be notified by state on basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reservation for OBCs in Educational Institutions – 93rd Amendment Act of 2005
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 – 27% quota for OBCs in central higher educational institutions including IITs and IIMs
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: April 2008 – Supreme Court upheld validity of Amendment Act and OBC Quota Act
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court directed exclusion of ‘creamy layer’ among OBCs
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Components of creamy layer among OBCs (constitutional post holders, Group A/B officers, military ranks, professionals, business persons, high income/wealth)
children: Persons holding constitutional posts (President, VP, Judges, UPSC/SPSC members, CEC, CAG, etc.)
Group A/Class I and Group B/Class II officers of All India, Central and State Services; equivalent in PSUs, Banks, Insurance, Universities, private employment
Persons of rank colonel and above in Army, equivalent in Navy, Air Force, Paramilitary
Professionals like doctors, lawyers, engineers, artists, authors, consultants
Persons engaged in trade, business, industry
People holding agricultural land above certain limit or vacant land/buildings in urban areas
Persons with gross annual income more than ₹8 lakh or possessing wealth above exemption limit
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Evolution of creamy layer income ceiling: ₹1 lakh (1993), ₹2.5 lakh (2004), ₹4.5 lakh (2008), ₹6 lakh (2013), ₹8 lakh (2017)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reservation for EWSs in Educational Institutions – 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Central government order (2019) providing 10% reservation to EWSs in admission to educational institutions
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: EWS benefit for persons not covered under existing SC, ST, OBC reservations
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Eligibility criteria for EWS: family gross annual income below ₹8 lakh from all sources for financial year prior to year of application
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Exclusion from EWS if family owns: 5 acres agricultural land and above; residential flat 1000 sq.ft. and above; residential plot 100 sq.yards and above in notified municipalities; residential plot 200 sq.yards and above in other areas
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Property held by family in different locations clubbed for EWS eligibility
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Family for EWS includes person seeking benefit, parents, siblings below 18, spouse, children below 18
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment – Article 16
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters of employment or appointment under State
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No discrimination on grounds of only religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence in public employment
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Four exceptions to Article 16
children: Exception (a): Parliament can prescribe residence as condition for certain employment in state/UT/local/other authority – Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act of 1957 expired in 1974; now only Andhra Pradesh (Article 371D) and Telangana (extended by Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014)
Exception (b): State can provide reservation for any backward class not adequately represented in state services
Exception (c): Law can provide that incumbent of office related to religious or denominational institution or its governing body should belong to particular religion or denomination
Exception (d): State can make provision for reservation of up to 10% appointments/posts for economically weaker sections – added by 103rd Amendment Act, 2019
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: EWS reservation in public employment: central government order (2019) providing 10% reservation in civil posts and services of Government of India
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Scientific and technical posts can be exempted from EWS reservation if: posts above lower grade in Group A; classified as scientific/technical per Cabinet Secretariat Order (1961); posts for conducting/organizing/guiding/directing research
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Mandal Commission and Aftermath
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: National Awards should not be used as suffixes or prefixes – otherwise forfeited
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: National Awards instituted in 1954; discontinued in 1977 by Janata Party government; revived in 1980 by Indira Gandhi government
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to Freedom – Article 19
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Six rights guaranteed to all citizens under Article 19
children: Right to freedom of speech and expression
Right to assemble peaceably and without arms
Right to form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Right to move freely throughout territory of India
Right to reside and settle in any part of territory of India
Right to practice any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Originally seven rights under Article 19 – right to acquire, hold and dispose of property deleted by 44th Amendment Act, 1978
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 19 rights protected against state action only, not private individuals
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 19 rights available only to citizens and shareholders of a company, not foreigners or legal persons
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: State can impose ‘reasonable’ restrictions only on grounds mentioned in Article 19 itself
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Speech and Expression – includes right to propagate own and others’ views; freedom of press; freedom of commercial advertisements; right against tapping of telephonic conversation; right to telecast (government has no monopoly on electronic media); right against bundh called by political party; right to know about government activities; freedom of silence; right against imposition of pre-censorship on newspaper; right to demonstration or picketing but not right to strike
children: Right to propagate own and others’ views
Freedom of press
Freedom of commercial advertisements
Right against tapping of telephonic conversation
Right to telecast (government has no monopoly on electronic media)
Right against bundh called by political party
Right to know about government activities
Freedom of silence
Right against imposition of pre-censorship on newspaper
Right to demonstration or picketing but not right to strike
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech and expression on grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India, security of state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Assembly – right to hold public meetings, demonstrations, take out processions; must be peaceful and unarmed; does not include right to strike
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on assembly on grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India, public order (including maintenance of traffic)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Section 144 of Criminal Procedure Code (1973) – magistrate can restrain assembly, meeting or procession if risk of obstruction, annoyance, danger to life/health/safety, disturbance of public tranquillity, riot or affray
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Section 141 of Indian Penal Code – assembly of five or more persons becomes unlawful if object is to resist execution of law/legal process, forcibly occupy property, commit mischief/criminal trespass, force person to do illegal act, threaten government/officials exercising lawful powers
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Association – right to form political parties, companies, partnership firms, societies, clubs, organisations, trade unions, any body of persons; includes right to start and continue association; covers negative right not to form or join
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on association on grounds of sovereignty and integrity of India, public order, morality
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to obtain recognition of association is not a fundamental right
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court: trade unions have no guaranteed right to effective bargaining, strike or lock-out; right to strike can be controlled by industrial law
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Movement – entitles every citizen to move freely throughout country (from one state to another or within state); promotes national feeling
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on movement on grounds of interests of general public and protection of interests of any scheduled tribe; entry of outsiders in tribal areas restricted to protect tribal culture, language, customs, traditional vocation and properties
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court: freedom of movement of prostitutes can be restricted on ground of public health and public morals; Bombay High Court validated restrictions on movement of persons affected by AIDS
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Two dimensions of freedom of movement: internal (right to move inside country – Article 19); external (right to move out and come back – Article 21)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Residence – right to reside (temporarily) and settle (permanently) in any part of country; removes internal barriers; promotes nationalism
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on residence on grounds of interest of general public and protection of interests of scheduled tribes; tribals permitted to regulate property rights according to customary rules
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court: certain areas can be banned for prostitutes and habitual offenders regarding residence and movement
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to residence and right to movement are overlapping and complementary
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Profession, etc. – right to practice any profession, carry on any occupation, trade or business; covers all means of earning livelihood
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Reasonable restrictions on profession, trade, business in interest of general public; State can prescribe professional/technical qualifications
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: State can carry on any trade, business, industry or service to exclusion (complete or partial) of citizens or otherwise – no requirement to justify monopoly
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right does not include immoral (trafficking in women/children) or dangerous (harmful drugs/explosives) occupations – State can absolutely prohibit or regulate through licensing
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibition of traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour) and other similar forms of forced labour; contravention is an offence punishable by law
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right under Article 23 available to both citizens and non-citizens; protects individual against State and private persons
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: ‘Traffic in human beings’ includes selling/buying men, women, children; immoral traffic including prostitution; devadasis; slavery
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 – to punish trafficking acts
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: ‘Begar’ means compulsory work without remuneration – Indian system under zamindars forcing tenants
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: ‘Forced labour’ includes compelling person to work against will; ‘force’ includes physical/legal force and compulsion of economic circumstances (working for less than minimum wage)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Related laws against forced labour: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976; Minimum Wages Act, 1948; Contract Labour Act, 1970; Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
children: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
Minimum Wages Act, 1948
Contract Labour Act, 1970
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Exception under Article 23: State can impose compulsory service for public purposes (military or social service) without pay; but no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste or class
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibition of Employment of Children in Factories, etc. – Article 24
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any factory, mine or other hazardous activities (construction, railway); does not prohibit employment in harmless or innocent work
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 – most important law relating to child labour
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Other laws prohibiting child labour: Employment of Children Act, 1938; Factories Act, 1948; Mines Act, 1952; Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; Plantation Labour Act, 1951; Motor Transport Workers Act, 1951; Apprentices Act, 1961; Bidi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966; and other similar acts
children: Employment of Children Act, 1938
Factories Act, 1948
Mines Act, 1952
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
Plantation Labour Act, 1951
Motor Transport Workers Act, 1951
Apprentices Act, 1961
Bidi and Cigar Workers Act, 1966
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: 1996 – Supreme Court directed establishment of Child Labour Rehabilitation Welfare Fund with offending employer depositing fine of ₹20,000 per child employed; directions for improvement of education, health, nutrition of children
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 – established National Commission and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights and Children’s Courts for speedy trial of offences against children
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: 2006 – government banned employment of children as domestic servants or workers in hotels, dhabas, restaurants, shops, factories, resorts, spas, tea-shops, etc.; warning of prosecution and penal action
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 – amended 1986 Act; renamed as Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to Freedom of Religion – Articles 25-28
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice and Propagation of Religion – Article 25
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: All persons equally entitled to freedom of conscience and right to freely profess, practice and propagate religion
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom of conscience – inner freedom to mould relation with God/Creatures; right to profess – declaration of religious beliefs openly and freely; right to practice – performance of worship, rituals, ceremonies, exhibition of beliefs; right to propagate – transmission of religious beliefs to others; does not include right to convert; forcible conversions impinge on freedom of conscience
children: Freedom of conscience – inner freedom to mould relation with God/Creatures
Right to profess – declaration of religious beliefs openly and freely
Right to practice – performance of worship, rituals, ceremonies, exhibition of beliefs
Right to propagate – transmission of religious beliefs to others; does not include right to convert; forcible conversions impinge on freedom of conscience
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 25 covers both religious beliefs (doctrines) and religious practices (rituals)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Rights under Article 25 available to all persons – citizens and non-citizens; subject to public order, morality, health and other fundamental rights provisions
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: State can regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: State can provide for social welfare and reform or throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Explanations under Article 25: wearing and carrying of kirpans included in profession of Sikh religion; Hindus include Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs – Article 26
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Every religious denomination or its section has rights under Article 26: establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; manage own affairs in matters of religion; own and acquire movable and immovable property; administer such property in accordance with law
children: Right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes
Right to manage own affairs in matters of religion
Right to own and acquire movable and immovable property
Right to administer such property in accordance with law
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 25 guarantees individual rights; Article 26 guarantees collective freedom of religion of denominations
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Rights under Article 26 subject to public order, morality and health (not subject to other fundamental rights provisions)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court conditions for religious denomination: collection of individuals with system of beliefs conducive to spiritual well-being; common organisation; distinctive name
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Ramakrishna Mission and Ananda Marga held to be religious denominations within Hindu religion; Aurobindo Society not a religious denomination
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom from Taxation for Promotion of a Religion – Article 27
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No person compelled to pay any taxes for promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination; State should not spend public money collected by tax for promotion of particular religion
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibits State from favouring, patronising, supporting one religion over another; taxes can be used for promotion or maintenance of all religions
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 27 prohibits levy of a tax, not a fee; fee can be levied on pilgrims for special services/safety measures; fee on religious endowments for regulation expenditure
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Freedom from Attending Religious Instruction – Article 28
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No religious instruction in educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Exception: institution administered by State but established under endowment or trust requiring imparting of religious instruction is permitted
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: In institutions recognised by State or receiving aid, no person required to attend religious instruction or worship without consent; for minor, guardian's consent needed
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Four types of institutions under Article 28: (a) wholly maintained by State – religious instruction prohibited; (b) administered by State but established under endowment/trust – religious instruction permitted; (c) recognised by State; (d) receiving aid from State – (c) and (d) religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
children: Institution wholly maintained by State – religious instruction prohibited
Institution administered by State but established under endowment/trust – religious instruction permitted
Institution recognised by State – religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
Institution receiving aid from State – religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Cultural and Educational Rights – Articles 29-30
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Protection of Interests of Minorities – Article 29
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Any section of citizens residing in any part of India having distinct language, script or culture shall have right to conserve the same
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No citizen denied admission into any educational institution maintained by State or receiving aid on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: First provision of Article 29 protects group rights; second protects individual rights
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 29 protects both religious and linguistic minorities; Supreme Court: scope not restricted to minorities – words 'section of citizens' include majority
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to conserve language includes right to agitate for protection; political speeches/promises for conservation of language not corrupt practice under Representation of the People Act, 1951
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right of Minorities to Establish and Administer Educational Institutions – Article 30
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: All minorities (religious or linguistic) shall have right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Compensation amount fixed by State for compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institution shall not restrict or abrogate right – added by 44th Amendment Act, 1978
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: In granting aid, State shall not discriminate against any educational institution managed by minority
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Protection under Article 30 only for minorities (religious or linguistic), not any section of citizens as under Article 29
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Term 'minority' not defined anywhere in Constitution
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right under Article 30 includes right to impart education to children in own language
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Three types of minority educational institutions: (a) seeking recognition and aid; (b) seeking only recognition; (c) seeking neither recognition nor aid
children: Institutions seeking recognition and aid – subject to State regulatory power for syllabus, academic standards, discipline, sanitation, employment of teaching staff, etc.
Institutions seeking only recognition – subject to State regulatory power for syllabus, academic standards, discipline, sanitation, employment of teaching staff, etc.
Institutions seeking neither recognition nor aid – free to administer affairs subject to general laws (contract, labour, industrial, tax, economic regulations)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Secretary of Malankara Syrian Catholic College case (2007) – Supreme Court summarised general principles regarding Article 30
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Principles under Article 30: right includes choice of governing body, appointment of teaching/non-teaching staff, action for dereliction of duty, admission of eligible students, setting fee structure, use of properties
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right under Article 30 ensures equality with majority, not reverse discrimination; general laws apply equally
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right under Article 30 not absolute; does not include right to maladminister; regulatory measures for educational standards and academic excellence allowed
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Regulations concerning welfare of students/teachers, eligibility criteria, qualifications, conditions of service, prevention of exploitation, syllabus/curriculum do not interfere with Article 30(1)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Unaided minority educational institutions have freedom to appoint teachers by rational procedure subject to eligibility/qualifications
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Extension of aid does not alter nature of minority institution; conditions can be imposed to ensure proper utilization without diluting right
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Right to Constitutional Remedies – Article 32
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Article 32 confers right to remedies for enforcement of fundamental rights – in itself a fundamental right
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 most important article, 'the very soul and heart of the Constitution'
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court ruled Article 32 is a basic feature of Constitution – cannot be abridged or taken away even by amendment
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Provisions of Article 32: (a) right to move Supreme Court for enforcement; (b) Supreme Court can issue directions/orders/writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto); (c) Parliament can empower any other court (excluding high courts as Article 226 already confers power) to issue writs; (d) right to move Supreme Court cannot be suspended except as provided (President can suspend during national emergency under Article 359)
children: Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights
Supreme Court can issue directions/orders/writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto)
Parliament can empower any other court (excluding high courts) to issue writs
Right to move Supreme Court cannot be suspended except as provided (President can suspend during national emergency under Article 359)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court is defender and guarantor of fundamental rights – vested with original and wide powers
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Purpose of Article 32: guaranteed, effective, expeditious, inexpensive, summary remedy
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Only fundamental rights can be enforced under Article 32, not other rights; violation of a fundamental right is sine qua non for exercise of Article 32
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court under Article 32 cannot determine question not involving fundamental rights
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court under Article 32 is original but not exclusive – concurrent with high court under Article 226
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: High courts also have original powers under Article 226 to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Aggrieved party can move either high court or Supreme Court directly
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Availability of alternate remedy is no bar to relief under Article 32 (since it is a fundamental right)
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court ruled where relief through high court available under Article 226, aggrieved party should first move high court
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Writs – Types and Scope
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Supreme Court (Article 32) and high courts (Article 226) can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Parliament (under Article 32) can empower any other court to issue these writs – no such provision made so far
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Before 1950, only High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs; Article 226 now empowers all high courts
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Writs borrowed from English law – 'prerogative writs' issued in exercise of prerogative of King as fountain of justice
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Writ jurisdiction of Supreme Court vs high court: (1) Supreme Court only for fundamental rights; high court for fundamental rights and any other purpose – narrower for Supreme Court; (2) Supreme Court territorial jurisdiction throughout India; high court limited to its territorial jurisdiction or where cause of action arises within – wider for Supreme Court; (3) Remedy under Article 32 is a fundamental right, court may not refuse; remedy under Article 226 is discretionary, high court may refuse
children: Supreme Court only for fundamental rights; high court for fundamental rights and any other purpose – narrower for Supreme Court
Supreme Court territorial jurisdiction throughout India; high court limited to its territorial jurisdiction or where cause of action arises within – wider for Supreme Court
Remedy under Article 32 is a fundamental right, court may not refuse; remedy under Article 226 is discretionary, high court may refuse
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Habeas Corpus – Latin 'to have the body'; order to person detaining another to produce body before court; court examines cause and legality; sets free if illegal; bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention; can be issued against public authorities and private individuals; not issued where detention lawful, proceeding for contempt of legislature/court, detention by competent court, detention outside court's jurisdiction
children: Habeas corpus – order to person detaining another to produce body before court; court examines cause and legality; sets free if illegal
Bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention
Can be issued against public authorities and private individuals
Not issued where detention lawful, proceeding for contempt of legislature/court, detention by competent court, detention outside court's jurisdiction
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Mandamus – Latin 'we command'; command to public official to perform official duties failed or refused; can be issued against public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal, government; cannot be issued against private individual/body; to enforce departmental instruction without statutory force; when duty discretionary not mandatory; to enforce contractual obligation; against President of India or state governors; against Chief Justice of High Court acting in judicial capacity
children: Mandamus – command to public official to perform official duties failed or refused
Can be issued against public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal, government

Cannot be issued against private individual/body; to enforce departmental instruction without statutory force; when duty discretionary not mandatory; to enforce contractual obligation; against President of India or state governors; against Chief Justice of High Court acting in judicial capacity
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Prohibition – Latin 'to forbid'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction or usurping jurisdiction; directs inactivity; can be issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, not administrative, legislative, private individuals
children: Prohibition – higher court to lower court/tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction or usurping jurisdiction
Directs inactivity
Can be issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, not administrative, legislative, private individuals
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Certiorari – Latin 'to be certified'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to transfer pending case to itself or to squash order; grounds: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law; both preventive and curative; earlier only against judicial/quasi-judicial; 1991 Supreme Court ruled can be issued even against administrative authorities affecting rights; not available against legislative bodies and private individuals
children: Certiorari – higher court to lower court/tribunal to transfer pending case to itself or to squash order
Grounds: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law
Both preventive and curative
Earlier only against judicial/quasi-judicial; 1991 Supreme Court ruled can be issued even against administrative authorities affecting rights
Not available against legislative bodies and private individuals
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Quo-Warranto – Latin 'by what authority or warrant'; court enquires into legality of claim of person to public office; prevents illegal usurpation; can be issued only for substantive public office of permanent character created by statute or Constitution; not for ministerial or private office; can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved person
children: Quo-Warranto – court enquires into legality of claim of person to public office; prevents illegal usurpation
Can be issued only for substantive public office of permanent character created by statute or Constitution
Not for ministerial or private office
Can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved person
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Armed Forces and Fundamental Rights – Article 33
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Parliament can restrict or abrogate fundamental rights of members of armed forces, para-military forces, police forces, intelligence agencies and analogous forces to ensure proper discharge of duties and maintenance of discipline
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Power to make laws under Article 33 conferred only on Parliament, not state legislatures; such law cannot be challenged in any court on ground of contravention of fundamental rights
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Originally right to property under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 – one of seven fundamental rights; Article 19(1)(f) guaranteed right to acquire, hold, dispose of property; Article 31 guaranteed right against deprivation of property, provided no deprivation except by authority of law, empowered State to acquire/requisition property for public purpose and on payment of compensation

gaps.text: Criticism of Fundamental Rights
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Excessive limitations – subjected to innumerable exceptions, restrictions, qualifications, explanations; critics: Constitution grants rights with one hand and takes away with the other; Jaspat Roy Kapoor suggested renaming as 'Limitations on Fundamental Rights' or 'Fundamental Rights and Limitations Thereon'
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No social and economic rights – list mainly political rights; no provision for right to social security, right to work, right to employment, right to rest and leisure – these available in advanced democracies and erstwhile USSR/China
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No clarity – stated in vague, indefinite, ambiguous manner; phrases like 'public order', 'minorities', 'reasonable restriction', 'public interest' not clearly defined; language complicated; Sir Ivor Jennings called Constitution of India a 'paradise for lawyers'
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No permanency – Parliament can curtail or abolish (e.g., right to property in 1978); 'doctrine of basic structure' only limitation
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Suspension during Emergency – enforcement suspended during National Emergency (except Articles 20 and 21); critics: rights should be enjoyable in all situations
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Expensive remedy – judicial process too expensive for common man; rights benefit mainly rich section
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: Preventive detention – Article 22 takes away spirit and substance; confers arbitrary powers on State; negates individual liberty; no democratic country has made preventive detention integral part of Constitution as India
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: No consistent philosophy – chapter not product of philosophical principle; Sir Ivor Jennings: Fundamental Rights based on no consistent philosophy; creates difficulty for courts in interpretation

gaps.text: Article 21 as originally enacted uses the phrase 'procedure established by law', which is borrowed from the Japanese Constitution. Under this phrase, protection is available only against arbitrary executive action (no procedure), not against the legislature passing a law that may be unjust. This is in contrast to the American 'due process of law' which also tests the substantive fairness of the law.
gaps.subject: Polity

gaps.text: The American concept of 'due process of law' requires that laws and procedures for depriving a person of life or personal liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable, not merely enacted by a competent legislature. The Supreme Court in Menaka imported this principle to interpret Article 21 expansively.
gaps.subject: Polity
